rows.citation: Liu, J., Xia, C. S., Wang, Y., et al. (2023). Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? Rigorous Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Generation. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36, pp. 21558-21572.
rows.model_type: LLM-synthesised general-purpose Python functions (HumanEval / MBPP benchmark tasks); general software, not scientific models
rows.controlled_mutations: partial - mutants of ground-truth programs serve as a test-suite reduction requirement; inputs grown by type-aware mutation; no domain-specific single-fault families
rows.multiple_stimuli: yes - LLM-seeded plus type-aware-mutation input generation greatly expands test inputs per task (abstract reports 80x for HumanEval+)
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - outputs compared by differential testing against ground-truth implementation; no physiological features or calibrated tolerances
rows.protocol_optimization: yes - greedy set cover selects a minimal test subset preserving branch coverage, killed mutants and empirical LLM-sample kills (HumanEval+-mini)
rows.heldout_evaluation: partial - reduction tool README mentions per-LLM cross-validation output; no held-out program or fault-family split verified in paper text read
rows.ai_transformations: yes - measures how thin tests let wrong LLM-generated code pass; generation from specifications, not edits of existing code
rows.software: EvalPlus - https://github.com/evalplus/evalplus (Apache-2.0 per GitHub API); reduction code in tools/tsr
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Closest structural analogue in this batch: test augmentation plus greedy mutant-kill set cover. NeuroSem transfers the idea to neuron models: current-clamp protocols as tests, eFEL features with refinement-calibrated tolerances as oracle, domain single-fault mutants of existing NeuroML models, count/runtime-matched random baselines, held-out models and mutation family. Greedy mutant-coverage selection itself is not novel.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (title, 4 authors, NeurIPS 36, pages); DataCite for arXiv 10.48550/arxiv.2305.01210 abstract; arXiv abs page and arXiv HTML full text (sections 2.1-2.2, test-suite reduction); GitHub REST API via gh (repo licence) and README + tools/tsr/README.md
rows.found_via: Crossref silent semantic errors LLM code query; verified via Crossref

rows.citation: DiMattina, C., & Zhang, K. (2013). Adaptive stimulus optimization for sensory systems neuroscience. Frontiers in Neural Circuits, 7, 101.
rows.model_type: sensory neuron response models (firing-rate, generalized linear, multilayer network and some biophysical models) probed in neurophysiology experiments
rows.controlled_mutations: no - compares competing candidate models of a sensory neuron; no deliberate single-fault mutants of a reference model
rows.multiple_stimuli: yes - reviews adaptive generation of stimulus sequences and ensembles (optimal, iso-response, system-identification paradigms)
rows.electrophysiology_features: partial - responses summarised mainly as firing rates or spike counts; no current-clamp feature battery such as sag, latency or AP shape
rows.protocol_optimization: yes - stimuli chosen online to maximise information for parameter estimation or to discriminate competing models (information-theoretic or likelihood criteria)
rows.heldout_evaluation: no - narrative review; no held-out model or held-out fault-family evaluation design
rows.ai_transformations: no - no AI-assisted code or model transformations
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Conceptual precedent for choosing stimuli that separate models. NeuroSem instead selects a fixed offline current-clamp battery by greedy coverage over discovery mutants to detect regressions between a reference and a transformed simulation model, with frozen tolerances and held-out evaluation, rather than adaptive in-experiment model estimation or comparison.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (title, authors, volume 7, Frontiers Media); Europe PMC REST search (abstract, PMID 23761737, PMCID PMC3674314, article 101); Europe PMC fullTextXML (section headings; biophysical-model and model-comparison sections read)
rows.found_via: Europe PMC stimulus design + model discrimination query; verified via Crossref + abstract

rows.citation: Yan, S., & Zhu, H. (2025). Metamorphic Testing on Scientific Programs for Solving Second-Order Elliptic Differential Equations. Software Testing, Verification and Reliability, 35(1), e1912.
rows.model_type: scientific computing programs solving second-order elliptic PDEs (general scientific software without exact oracles)
rows.controlled_mutations: unclear - abstract reports detection of faults common in scientific programs; full text blocked, so fault-seeding method (e.g. mutants) unverified
rows.multiple_stimuli: partial - metamorphic relations derived from the numerical model generate related follow-up test inputs; no stimulation protocols
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - PDE solver outputs checked against metamorphic relations; no electrophysiology
rows.protocol_optimization: no - abstract describes deriving metamorphic relations and a testing process; no test-set selection under a budget reported
rows.heldout_evaluation: unclear - full text inaccessible (Wiley 403); abstract only reports comparison against the trend method
rows.ai_transformations: no - no AI-generated or AI-edited programs mentioned in abstract
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Oracle here is formally derived metamorphic relations for PDE solvers. NeuroSem uses differential comparison of a transformed neuron model against its reference over current-clamp protocols, with tolerances calibrated by time-step refinement, plus greedy protocol selection and held-out models/mutation family. Metamorphic testing of scientific software is not NeuroSem's novelty.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (title, 2 authors, vol 35 issue 1, article e1912, published online 2024-12-22, print issue 2025-01, abstract, reference list); OpenAlex works API (metadata consistent, hybrid OA); Wiley landing and full-text pages returned HTTP 403 to curl and WebFetch
rows.found_via: Crossref 'metamorphic testing scientific simulation software'; verified via Crossref abstract

rows.citation: Birchler, C., Ganz, N., Khatiri, S., et al. (2022). Cost-effective Simulation-based Test Selection in Self-driving Cars Software. arXiv preprint arXiv:2211.11409.
rows.model_type: self-driving car software tested with generated road scenarios in the BeamNG.tech simulator (cyber-physical system)
rows.controlled_mutations: no - faults are lane departures of the driving agent under generated scenarios and risk-factor settings; no seeded single-fault mutants
rows.multiple_stimuli: yes - thousands of generated simulation tests (abstract reports 22,652 across two datasets)
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - road-geometry input features extracted before execution; no physiological features
rows.protocol_optimization: yes - ML classifiers predict unsafe tests so only likely-failing ones run; cost-effectiveness is unsafe tests per simulation time versus random selection
rows.heldout_evaluation: partial - 10-fold cross-validation or a separate testing dataset for classifiers; no held-out system or fault family
rows.ai_transformations: no - machine learning used for test selection; no AI-generated code edits
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Analogue for budget-aware simulation test selection with a random baseline normalised by runtime. NeuroSem selects one fixed protocol battery by greedy coverage over a mutant-by-protocol detection matrix, compares count- and runtime-matched random sets, and tests generalisation to unseen neuron models and a held-out mutation family, rather than per-test ML outcome prediction for one system.
rows.verification_method: DataCite DOI API (title, 5 creators, 2022, abstract); arXiv abs page (authors, v1 2022-11-21, cs.SE, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); arXiv HTML full text (sections 2-4; its header names Science of Computer Programming, published version not verified); GitHub REST API via gh and README
rows.found_via: DataCite (arXiv DOIs) test selection + simulation title query

rows.citation: Tian, M., Gao, L., Zhang, S., et al. (2024). SciCode: A Research Coding Benchmark Curated by Scientists. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37, pp. 30624-30650.
rows.model_type: LLM code-generation benchmark of research problems (numerical methods, system simulation, scientific calculation across 16 natural-science subfields)
rows.controlled_mutations: no - problems are scored against scientist-annotated gold solutions; no mutation of existing models
rows.multiple_stimuli: partial - several numeric test cases per subproblem; not stimulation protocols or perturbation batteries
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - numeric outputs compared to frozen targets; no electrophysiology features
rows.protocol_optimization: no - fixed test cases; no selection of a compact test battery
rows.heldout_evaluation: partial - models evaluated on benchmark problems with gold test data; no held-out model or fault-family design relevant to transformations
rows.ai_transformations: yes - evaluates language models generating scientific code from problem descriptions, not edits of existing neuron models
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Relevant only to NeuroSem's optional agent case study as a hidden numeric-test benchmark. NeuroSem asks whether edits to existing NeuroML models preserve behaviour across perturbation protocols with calibrated tolerances; SciCode scores from-scratch scientific code generation against fixed targets.
rows.verification_method: Crossref works API (title, 30 authors, NeurIPS 37, pages); DataCite for arXiv 10.48550/arxiv.2407.13168 (abstract); arXiv abs page (author list, CC BY 4.0); GitHub REST API via gh (licence) and README (NeurIPS D&B 2024 acceptance note)
rows.found_via: Crossref SciCode query; DataCite (arXiv); GitHub scicode-bench/SciCode (Apache-2.0)

rows.citation: Hu, S., Huang, L., Deng, Y., et al. (2026). SciCode-Verified: How Benchmark Defects Underestimated the Scientific-Coding Ability of Language Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2608.04975.
rows.model_type: audit and correction of an LLM scientific-coding benchmark (hidden numeric tests)
rows.controlled_mutations: no - audits and corrects benchmark specifications, gold answers and tests; no seeded faults in models
rows.multiple_stimuli: no - reuses SciCode's per-subproblem test cases; no stimulation protocols
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - numeric closeness checks against frozen targets; no electrophysiology
rows.protocol_optimization: no - tests corrected or tightened by expert audit, not selected by optimisation
rows.heldout_evaluation: partial - twelve model snapshots re-evaluated on corrected data with harness held fixed; no discovery/held-out split for test design
rows.ai_transformations: yes - evaluates LLM-generated scientific code; reports misgrading from non-reproducible gold answers and over-tight tolerances (unreviewed preprint claims)
rows.software: SciCode-Verified - https://github.com/flyingwagner/scicode-verified (GitHub API detects no top-level licence; README badge links a vendored Apache-2.0 LICENSE file)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Cautionary evidence that hidden numeric tests with poorly calibrated tolerances or non-deterministic gold answers misgrade solutions; supports NeuroSem's refinement-calibrated tolerances, determinism checks and audited answer keys for its agent case study. It does not test behaviour preservation of model transformations.
rows.verification_method: DataCite DOI API (title, 4 creators, abstract, submitted 2026-08-05); arXiv abs page (authors, cs.SE/cs.AI, comments); GitHub REST API via gh (repo metadata, file list, vendored LICENSE header) and README + CLEANING_LOG.md
